discovery: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany

nominees.name: Jean Dalibard
nominees.affiliation: Collège de France and Laboratoire Kastler Brossel, ENS-PSL, Paris, France

nominees.name: Peter Zoller
nominees.affiliation: University of Innsbruck and IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Austria

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum many-body physics
motivation: Feynman proposed that quantum systems might best be understood by simulating them with other, controllable quantum systems. The nominees turned this idea into an experimental science. Zoller, with Jaksch and co-workers, showed theoretically that atoms in optical lattices realise the Bose-Hubbard model and can be tuned across a quantum phase transition. Bloch observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition (2002) and went on to pioneer single-atom-resolved quantum gas microscopy, many-body localisation and studies of entanglement in lattice systems. Dalibard, a founder of sub-recoil laser cooling, demonstrated the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in two-dimensional atomic gases and developed artificial gauge fields for neutral atoms, opening topological matter to cold-atom experiments. Together they made ultracold atoms a clean, tunable laboratory for condensed-matter questions that are otherwise intractable. This is a central pillar of the second quantum revolution, built on individual control of quantum particles.
